$comment: Rules whose matcher is an engine check (matcher.type = structural). Metadata and wording live here; the logic lives in the engine and is covered by the engine's unit tests. Fields: id, cat, sev, conf, surf, sup (suppressible), check, exp, rem.
rules: A schema enum, default, const or example value reads like a sentence. Values like this are a known place to hide instructions for the AI.
Use short literal values. Put explanations in the description.
A schema property name is unusually long or reads like an instruction.
An instruction aimed at the AI appears only when separate metadata fields are read together.
Remove the instruction from every field involved.
The text contains invisible characters (such as zero-width spaces) that a person reading it can't see.
The text contains bidirectional control characters that can make it display differently from how it reads to a machine.
Remove the bidirectional override, embedding and isolate characters.
The text contains Unicode tag characters, which are invisible but can carry hidden instructions.
A word mixes letters from different scripts (for example Latin and Cyrillic), a common way to imitate another name.
Use a single script in each name and word.
The metadata contains terminal escape sequences that can hide or recolor text when displayed.
The metadata contains HTML or markdown comments, which most interfaces don't display.
The metadata contains an encoded blob (base64, hex or percent-encoding) that decodes to text.
Remove encoded content from metadata, or explain what it is.
The text contains a long run of blank space followed by more text, which pushes content out of view.
The tool output contains terminal escape sequences that can hide or recolor text.
Strip escape sequences before showing the output.
The metadata contains a large encoded blob (256 characters or more) that decodes to text.
The metadata gives instructions about another tool (one this server doesn't provide), which can change how the AI uses that other tool.
Describe only this server's own tools.
A tool name matches or closely imitates a tool from another server.
What the tool is described as doing doesn't fit what it asks for (for example a time tool that takes a shell command).
Ask only for the inputs the tool needs, or describe the tool accurately.
The tool's safety annotations contradict its own name or description (for example marked read-only but named delete).
Make the annotations match what the tool is described as doing.
A tool or prompt has no description.
A tool whose name sounds destructive has no safety annotations.
Add annotations such as destructiveHint: true.
A tool has no input schema.
Add an inputSchema, even an empty object schema.
A tool name doesn't follow the MCP naming rules (1–128 characters: letters, digits, _ - .).
The JSON contains the same key twice. Different programs may read different values, so what you review may not be what runs.
The input contains invalid UTF-8 bytes.
The input uses a key such as __proto__ or constructor. It was handled as plain data.
Two tools have the same name, so clients may disagree about which one is called.
Give every tool a unique name.
The input contains an unpaired UTF-16 surrogate.
The input object had an accessor or unreadable property, which was not read.
The input object contains a cycle.
The input isn't valid JSON, so it couldn't be analyzed.
The input contained values that aren't JSON (functions, symbols, big integers or undefined). They were dropped.
The input doesn't have the expected shape. Analysis continued on the fields present.
The input is larger than the analysis limit, so it wasn't analyzed.
The input is nested deeper than the analysis limit.
The input has more values than the analysis limit.
The server lists more tools than the analysis limit; the rest weren't scanned.
Split the server or reduce its tool count.
A description is longer than 16 KiB. Real descriptions are almost never this long, and length is a known way to hide content.
A field is longer than the scan window; only its beginning and end were scanned.
The decoding budget ran out, so some encoded content wasn't decoded.
There were more findings than the report limit; the lowest-severity ones were dropped.
Fix the reported findings and scan again.
This command can't be fully analyzed statically (for example it builds the command at run time or uses eval), so what it will do is unknown.
Write the command out literally, or approve it after reading it.
This command downloads content and runs it as a script.
Download the script, read it, then run the saved copy.
This command redirects data to /dev/tcp or /dev/udp, which opens a network connection without a network tool.
Use a normal network tool so the destination is visible.
This command would delete or overwrite a whole filesystem, home directory or disk.
Target a specific path inside the project instead.
This SQL statement updates or deletes rows without a meaningful WHERE clause, so it affects every row.
Add a WHERE clause that selects only the rows you mean.
This SQL statement drops or truncates a table.
Make sure a backup exists and approve deliberately.
This action would change, move or delete a file that controls the agent or Glassbox (for example agent settings or hooks).
Make this change yourself, outside the agent, if you intend it.

This action would change a file that makes code run later or grants access to this machine (shell startup files, SSH authorized keys, scheduled jobs, launch agents, startup folders, global git config).
If you need this change, make it yourself outside the agent.
This action would read a Glassbox credential file.
The agent never needs these files. If you need them, read them yourself.
This command changes Glassbox or agent protection settings (for example the approval mode, plugins or nested agent settings).
Run this command yourself in a terminal if you intend it.
This command reads a sensitive file and also makes a network call.
Check where the data is going before approving.
A credential is being sent in a call that reaches the network or publishes content.
Check that the destination is supposed to receive this credential.
This action reads a sensitive file (for example keys, cloud credentials or a .env file).
Approve only if the task needs this file.
A live credential (a private key, a live API key, or a database URL with a password) is being passed to a tool that can write or send data.
Keep credentials out of tool arguments. Reference them from a secret store or an environment variable instead.
A credential issued by one service is being passed to a tool from a different service.
Pass credentials only to the service that issued them.
A tool result names another tool in this session next to an instruction, trying to make the AI call it.
Treat this content as data, not instructions.
Earlier in this session, injected content named this tool. This call may be the result of that injection.
Check that you asked for this action.
This session read private data and untrusted content, and this call sends data out. That combination is how injected instructions exfiltrate data.
Check what is being sent and where before approving.
This session read private data and untrusted content, and this call sends a credential or sensitive file out.
Deny this call unless you started this transfer yourself.
This session saw untrusted content and touched secrets, and this call makes a network request.
A server asked the client to include conversation context in a sampling request.
A server asked for the client's root directories.
Allow only if the server needs to know your project folders.
A server sent a request of an unknown type.
The server says its tool list changed. Re-fetch and compare it with the approved list now.
Re-fingerprint the server and review any changes.
A tool was added since you approved this server.
Review the new tool before using it.
A tool was removed since you approved this server.
No action needed unless you relied on it.
A description changed since you approved this server. Changed descriptions are how approved tools get new hidden instructions.
Read the new description and re-approve only if it's what you expect.
A tool title changed since approval.
A tool's input schema now accepts more than when you approved it.
Review the new parameters before re-approving.
A tool's input schema now accepts less than before.
A tool's input schema changed in a way that can't be classified, so it's treated as widened.
Review the schema change before re-approving.
A tool's annotations now describe it as more dangerous than when you approved it (for example no longer read-only).
The server's instructions changed since approval.
Read the new instructions before re-approving.
The server's name or title changed since approval.
Check that this is still the server you meant to use.
A prompt or resource was added since approval.
A tool's output schema changed since approval.
The fingerprints can't be compared (different algorithm or incomplete), so changes can't be ruled out.
Re-fetch the full tool list and review it.
The server sent your client a different tool list from the one that was graded. The public grade doesn't apply to what you received. This can be innocent (an update since grading, or per-user tools).
Re-grade the server with the tool list your client receives.
The cached rule set failed its signature check and was rejected. Glassbox is using its built-in rules, and high-risk actions need approval for the rest of this session.
Reinstall or refresh the rules from the official source.
The cached rule set is older than one already seen and was rejected. Glassbox is using its built-in rules, and high-risk actions need approval for the rest of this session.
Refresh the rules from the official source.
No usable cached rule set was found, so the built-in rules are in use.
The rule set is past its expiry date. It's still used, but newer rules may exist.
Update the rules when you're online.
The server's session ids look short, sequential or low-entropy, which can make sessions guessable.
